UNICORN SQUAD · LESSON GUIDE

mBot Taxi

Program a robot taxi to find the fastest route across a mini city, one block of code at a time.

robotics coding mBlock

Lesson Overview

Goal: program an mBot robot.

Task setup: the task is solved in pairs. Each pair gets one mBot2 robot and one iPad with the mBlock app.

Theory: Programming a robot, step by step

A robot doesn't know anything on its own — it only ever does exactly what its program tells it to do, one instruction at a time, in the exact order you give them. This is called a sequence: the robot finishes each command completely before moving on to the next one.

Today's program starts with an event — a condition that tells the robot when to start running everything that follows (in our case, "when button A is pressed"). After that trigger, the robot works through a list of movement commands one by one — move forward this many centimetres, turn this many degrees — until the list runs out.

A trigger, followed by a sequence of steps executed in order: that idea is the foundation of nearly every robot and computer program, no matter how complex it eventually becomes.

Good to know

  • mBlock, the app used today, is built on Scratch — a visual programming language developed at MIT that uses colour-coded blocks instead of typed code, so beginners can build real programs by snapping pieces together.
  • Real self-driving taxis, already running in some cities today, rely on exactly the same building blocks as your robot: sensors to sense the world around them, and a program that decides how to move next based on what they detect.
  • The word robot comes from the Czech word robota, meaning forced labour — it was first used in a 1920 play about artificial workers.

Step 1: Build Your Mini City

SETUP

Tape out a city on the floor

  1. Find a larger open floor area, free of tables — push tables together if needed to clear the space. Place location cards on the floor: school, shop, stadium, home, pool, and so on.
  2. Use painter's tape to mark paths, roads, or streets between the locations. The layout can be a different shape too, but it's best to stick to right-angle turns — this makes the very first programming task much easier for the girls to understand. You can copy the example layout exactly, or vary the distances, or lay out the "streets" differently so the whole city area takes on a different shape.
Example location layout
Need to print more location names? A printable set is available here. If you'd rather make your own, that works just as well — students can write or draw their own locations on A4 paper with a marker instead of using the printed set.
Task, as explained to the kids

Your mBot robot is a taxi that transports passengers from one place to another. Your task is to find the fastest and shortest route to the requested destination for your taxi, and program that route.

For the instructor

The iPad password is 0090. Each pair gets one robot and one iPad. Give pairs the task of choosing one simple trajectory first — for example POOL→LIBRARY or HOME→CAFÉ (so there's just a single turn). If they handle that well, let them try more complex variants too, for example AIRPORT→PARK→SHOP, where a small stop needs to be made at the park.

Step 2: The Two Movement Blocks

To steer the mBot's movement, we only need two blocks from the mBot 2 Chassis category:

1. Move forward some distance

The distance in cm can be changed to whatever the route needs.

2. Turn in some direction

In this task we only use right-angle turning — the robot turns either left or right, by 90°. Use 180° when the robot needs to turn all the way around at a destination.

Step 3: Setting Up mBlock

SETUP

Connect the app to the robot

  1. Launch the mBlock app from the iPad (the iPad password is 0090).
  2. Choose Coding → Start immediately, create your first work (tap the "+" mark in the middle of the screen).
  3. Under Devices, choose CyberPi — this is the small control panel on top of the robot.
  4. Tap the checkmark in the top right corner to confirm.
  5. Then, under Extensions, choose mBot2 Shield (if it isn't downloaded yet, download it first, then add it).
    Note: the iPad needs to be connected to Wi-Fi in order to download the extension.

Step 4: Program & Test the Route

PROGRAMMING

Build the driving program

  1. Always start the program with the yellow block from the Events category, which decides when the robot runs the program. Here we use the condition "when button A is pressed". Button A is the square button on the robot's control panel — pressing it makes the robot start executing your program.
  2. Now drag the blue movement commands from the mBot2 Chassis category underneath the Events block, and arrange them in the order that matches the route you want to drive. The robot executes commands exactly in the order you add them to the program.
    The values in the commands (how many cm the robot should move forward) need to be measured and refined by the girls themselves, through testing. Encourage them to adjust the program as needed until the robot reaches the desired destination.

    For example, a route could look like this.

  3. Once the first program is ready, switch the robot on using the ON/OFF button on its side.
  4. Hold the iPad close to the robot. Tap the Bluetooth icon in the app's header and connect to the robot. Then make sure Upload Mode is selected, and tap the arrow button in the bottom right to send the program to the robot.
  5. Once the program has uploaded to the robot, press button A on the robot's control panel — the robot should start the movement you programmed for it.

Bonus: Make It More Taxi-Like

If movement commands alone aren't enough, and you'd like the robot to behave more like a real self-driving taxi, feel free to add other commands to the program too. For example, the robot could show its status with lights (a busy taxi shows a red light, a free taxi shows a green light), make stops for picking up and dropping off passengers, turn around to drive back the same way if needed, and so on.

Encourage students to come up with their own solutions and experiment with different commands. Below is a sample program with explanations, giving ideas for how to add more "taxi-like" features to the robot.

Print the code example from here

Tips for instructors

  • Start every pair with a one-turn route (e.g. POOL→LIBRARY) before letting them try a multi-stop trip — early success builds confidence fast.
  • Let the girls measure and adjust the "cm" values themselves through trial and error, rather than handing them the exact numbers.
  • Keep the iPad password (0090) written somewhere visible, for pairs who forget it mid-task.
  • Encourage pairs who finish early to add taxi-like touches — status lights, passenger stops, a U-turn — rather than rushing straight to a new route.

Troubleshooting

  • Robot won't connect over Bluetooth? Make sure the robot is switched on and the iPad is held close to it, then try the Bluetooth icon again.
  • Robot doesn't move at all after pressing button A? Check the program was actually uploaded (Upload Mode selected, arrow button tapped), not left sitting in Live mode.
  • Robot overshoots or undershoots a location? Adjust the "cm" value in that movement block and re-upload — this is expected, and part of the task.
  • Robot turns the wrong way? Double-check whether the block says "left" or "right," and swap it if needed.

Reflection

Keep it spoken and group-based — a quick conversation, not a worksheet.

1. What went well for you today?

If the group gets stuck, try
  • What was the trickiest part, and how did you work through it?
  • What are you most proud of?
  • When did you realise "now it's working"?

2. What did you learn today?

If the group gets stuck, try
  • What can you do now that you couldn't this morning?
  • If you had to teach one thing from today to a friend or sibling, what would it be?
  • Why does that matter — what is it useful for?

3. Where else could you use this?

If the group gets stuck, try
  • Does any school subject use similar thinking (e.g. maths, art, PE)? Which one, and how?
  • Have you used something like this before — at home or in a game?
  • Who else uses this in real life — what job might that be? (See the Career path section below for ideas.)
Notes for instructors: keep the discussion spoken and group-based rather than written or individual. The follow-up prompts are a fallback, not a script — if the group answers well on the first try, move on rather than working through the whole list.

Career path: who works with robots & code? For instructors — optional

If you enjoyed programming your taxi today, you're touching on a field full of real careers. For example:

  • Robotics Engineers — design and build the robots that carry out programmed tasks in the real world.
  • Software Developers — write the step-by-step instructions that tell computers and robots what to do.
  • Autonomous Vehicle Engineers — work on the sensors and software behind real self-driving cars and taxis.
  • Mechatronics Technicians — build and maintain the mechanical and electronic parts inside robots.
  • Logistics Planners — work out the fastest, most efficient routes for deliveries, taxis, and transport networks.
